The increasing use of information technology has transformed how businesses manage their daily operations, maintain records, and deliver services to customers. In the fitness industry, gym establishments perform various administrative activities, including membership registration, attendance monitoring, payment recording, inventory management, and report preparation. These activities require accurate and organized information to ensure efficient operations and reliable service delivery. As the number of transactions and membership records increases, the use of computerized management systems becomes an important consideration for establishments seeking to improve their administrative processes.

In this context, IronGrind: A Fitness Gym Membership and Operations Management System also relates to the Sustainable Development Goals through its support for organized gym operations and digital recordkeeping. In relation to SDG 3, Good Health and Well-being, the system supports the administration of gym services by helping members access their membership information and enabling authorized personnel to record attendance. It does not provide medical advice or fitness coaching. For SDG 8, Decent Work and Economic Growth, its organized membership, inventory, sales, and reporting records can support routine administrative work and operational review. In relation to SDG 9, Industry, Innovation, and Infrastructure, IronGrind applies web-based technology to the operational needs of a local fitness establishment. The system also relates to SDG 12, Responsible Consumption and Production, by supporting digital membership, attendance, payment, and inventory records that can reduce reliance on paper forms and logbooks. These connections describe the intended contribution of the system rather than measured outcomes of SDG achievement.

Several gym management systems have been developed to support the operational requirements of fitness establishments. For instance, GymMaster describes membership management, billing, point-of-sale, online sign-ups, and access-control features

(GymMaster, n.d.). Similarly, GYMMANAGER describes sales, front-desk operations, scheduling, access control, and reporting within a centralized platform (GYMMANAGER, n.d.-a, n.d.-b). These platforms demonstrate the application of information systems in managing gym operations, particularly in organizing membership records, monitoring attendance, and recording business transactions.

Despite the availability of digital management solutions, establishments that rely on manual recordkeeping may encounter difficulties in maintaining accurate and accessible information. Paper-based registration forms, attendance logbooks, and separate files can make record retrieval time-consuming and increase the possibility of incomplete, duplicated, or misplaced information. These limitations may affect the efficiency of administrative activities, particularly when staff need to verify membership status, update transactions, monitor attendance, or prepare reports. The use of separate recording methods may also make it difficult to maintain consistent information across different operational activities.

Iron Grind Fitness Gym, located in Purok Mangga, Sulangon, Dapitan City, Zamboanga del Norte, provides fitness services to individuals with varying fitness goals. The establishment offers membership plans, fitness-related guidance, supplements, and gym merchandise. Its daily operations involve managing member registrations, processing membership renewals, recording payments, monitoring attendance, maintaining product inventory, and documenting sales transactions. These interconnected activities require systematic recordkeeping to support the gym owner and staff in managing the establishment effectively.

One of the operational concerns of Iron Grind Fitness Gym involves the management of membership information and transactions. When registration details, membership renewals, payment records, and membership periods are maintained through paper forms or separate files, staff may experience difficulties in organizing and retrieving information. Verifying whether a member has an active membership, confirming renewal payments, and determining membership expiration dates may require checking multiple records. Manual updating of membership information may also result in incomplete records, inconsistent entries, and delays in processing member transactions. These
concerns highlight the need for a more organized approach to managing membership information and maintaining accurate membership histories.

Attendance monitoring presents another operational concern. The use of handwritten attendance logbooks may result in unclear, duplicated, or missing entries, making it difficult to maintain accurate records of members' check-ins and check-outs. Staff may need to review attendance records manually when verifying member visits or preparing attendance reports. Without a centralized attendance monitoring mechanism, retrieving historical attendance information and ensuring consistency between attendance and membership records may become challenging.

In addition to membership and attendance management, the gym also handles the sale of supplements and merchandise. Its inventory includes powder, liquid, capsule, and tablet supplements tracked using the applicable weight, volume, piece, or box units, and merchandise such as shirts available in different sizes. Maintaining these products through manual inventory and sales records may create difficulties in monitoring available quantities, recording transactions, and identifying items that require restocking. Since the establishment processes payments in person rather than through an online payment facility, it also requires an organized recording mechanism that supports its existing payment procedures while maintaining accurate sales and inventory information.

The interconnected nature of these operational concerns emphasizes the need for a centralized information system that can integrate membership management, attendance monitoring, payment recording, inventory management, and reporting. Although commercial gym management platforms provide similar functionalities, Iron Grind Fitness Gym requires a solution designed around its specific operational processes, including membership applications and renewals approved by authorized staff or the administrator, staff-operated attendance recording, inventory tracking using product-appropriate units, and the recording of in-person transactions.

To address these concerns, the proponents developed IronGrind: A Fitness Gym Membership and Operations Management System. The system provides online membership registration, membership application review and approval, membership status monitoring, renewal requests, and member record management. It also incorporates QR

code-based attendance monitoring, allowing authorized staff to record member check-ins and check-outs. Members can access their dashboard to view their membership status, remaining membership period, attendance history, and QR code.

Furthermore, the system supports product inventory management, sales recording, membership transaction monitoring, and report generation. Its inventory features accommodate supplements monitored by weight, volume, piece, or box, as appropriate, and merchandise monitored by item and stock quantity. The system maintains the gym's existing in-person payment process while providing a digital mechanism for recording transactions. Supabase is utilized for authentication and database management, with role-based access controls to support the appropriate use of administrator, staff, and member functions.

Through the development of IronGrind, the proponents aim to provide a web-based information system that addresses the operational needs of Iron Grind Fitness Gym. By integrating its essential administrative activities into a centralized platform, the system is intended to minimize difficulties associated with manual recordkeeping, improve the organization and retrieval of information, support accurate membership and attendance monitoring, and facilitate inventory and transaction management. Ultimately, the project seeks to provide a practical and accessible technological solution that supports more efficient gym operations and improved service delivery to its members.

At present, gym operations involving member registration, membership renewals, payment recording, attendance monitoring, and supplement and merchandise sales may be handled through manual records such as logbooks, paper forms, and separate files. Member information, including contact details, membership plan, payment status, membership dates, and membership status, may be difficult to organize and retrieve when records are not maintained in one centralized system. This can result in delayed transactions, incomplete records, misplaced documents, and errors when updating information.

One major challenge is monitoring membership information, payments, and renewal requests. The administrator needs to review member records, determine membership status, confirm payment records, and monitor expiration dates. Members may

submit renewal requests at any time, but each request must be reviewed by authorized staff or the administrator before it takes effect. When records are managed manually, checking these details may take time and affect the speed of customer service. Attendance monitoring through a handwritten logbook can also lead to unclear, duplicate, incomplete, or missing entries.

Supplement and merchandise inventory and sales are also important in the daily operations of Iron Grind Fitness Gym. The gym sells supplements using product-appropriate weight, volume, piece, or box units and merchandise, such as shirts, by item and stock quantity. Manual records may make it difficult for the gym admin to monitor available quantities, record purchases accurately, identify items that need restocking, and review sales information for members and walk-in customers. Since the gym handles payments in person, it also needs an organized way to record completed transactions.

The IronGrind: A Fitness Gym Membership and Operations Management System was developed to address these concerns. The system brings together member and membership management, registration and renewal application review, payment recording, QR code-based attendance monitoring, product inventory, in-person sales transactions, and reports in one web-based platform.

The system organizes member profiles, membership plans, membership dates, and membership status. It allows applicants to submit registration details online for authorized staff or administrator review and allows existing members to submit renewal requests at any time. A renewal takes effect only after authorized staff or administrator approval. If the membership is still active, unused time is carried forward from its current expiry date; if it has expired, the renewed period starts on the approval date.

The system also assigns a QR code to each member. Authorized staff can scan the code to record a member’s check-in or check-out. Members can access their dashboard to view their membership status, membership-period progress, attendance history, and QR code.

Furthermore, the system allows the gym admin to manage supplements tracked using product-appropriate units and merchandise tracked by item and stock quantity. It records completed in-person sales for members and walk-in customers. The system
organizes membership, payment, attendance, inventory, and sales information into reports for the gym admin. It does not process payments online.

Therefore, this study aimed to develop a web-based system for Iron Grind Fitness Gym that organizes its membership and operational records. Through the IronGrind system, the gym admin can manage member information, review applications and renewal requests, record attendance and in-person transactions, monitor inventory, and review reports. This can reduce reliance on separate manual records and support more organized day-to-day operations.

The goal of this study was to design and develop IronGrind: A Fitness Gym Membership and Operations Management System for Iron Grind Fitness Gym. The system addresses the need to organize member information, membership applications and renewals, payments, attendance, product inventory, sales transactions, and reports.

To develop a member and membership management feature that creates a centralized database for member profiles, contact information, membership plans, membership start dates, expiration dates, and active or expired membership status.

To develop online registration and renewal request features that allow authorized staff and administrators to review, approve, or reject applications. Members may submit renewal requests at any time, but renewals take effect only after approval by authorized staff or the administrator. An active membership carries forward unused time, while an expired membership restarts on the approval date.
To develop a QR code-based attendance monitoring feature that allows authorized staff to record member check-ins and check-outs.

To develop a product inventory and sales feature that manages supplements tracked by weight, volume, piece, or box, as appropriate, and merchandise tracked by item and stock quantity, and records in-person transactions for members and walk-in customers.

To develop a reporting feature that organizes system data into separate membership, payment, attendance, inventory, and sales reports, allowing the gym admin to monitor each area of operations individually.

The study focused on the development of IronGrind: A Fitness Gym Membership and Operations Management System for Iron Grind Fitness Gym. The system provided a centralized platform for managing member profiles, membership applications and renewals, payments, attendance, product inventory, sales transactions, and reports.

The system stored member profiles and membership information, including plans, membership dates, and status. Applicants could submit online registration details for authorized staff or administrator review. Members could submit online renewal requests at any time, with approval required before a request took effect. Approval of an online renewal extended an active subscription from its current expiry date; an expired subscription restarted on the approval date. Direct counter renewal and active-member plan changes were separate operator transactions using the permitted plan, price, and membership dates.

The system included QR code-based attendance monitoring. Authorized administrators and staff could record member check-ins and check-outs using a supported computer or phone camera. Staff could also search by member name or Gmail, select the matching record, and submit attendance using its unique member identifier. Search alone did not record attendance or provide general member-profile access. A phone required an authorized operator sign-in and an administrator-managed pairing. Each phone browser installation used its own pairing QR and record. A setup QR expired after ten minutes; successful phone pairing remained valid for thirty days unless removed earlier. Paired phones and unexpired pending QRs shared the configured slot limit, initially set to two. A pending QR reserved one slot until paired, ended, or expired. The attendance scanner could be opened through a separate installation link and installed as a Progressive Web App; reinstalling in the same browser could reuse an available, active saved pairing. Cleared browser data, removed pairings, or expired connections could require administrator-assisted pairing again. Attendance without a check-out from a previous Philippine calendar date was displayed as Incomplete; the system did not invent a missing check-out timestamp.

The system also included product inventory and sales features. Supplements were tracked by weight, volume, piece, or box, as appropriate, while merchandise was tracked by item and stock quantity. The gym admin could manage product information and record in-person sales for members and walk-in customers. The system recorded transaction details but did not provide receipts. Payments were handled at the gym; the system did not process payments online.

Low-stock alerts used product-form and selling-unit rules, with conversion from the configured stock unit, including pounds, to the applicable base unit. Initial thresholds were 1,000 g for protein powder; 250 g for creatine, pre-workout, amino-acid, and vitamin powders; 500 g for other powders; 1,000 ml for liquids; 30 individually sold capsules or tablets; four boxes; ten other supplement items; and four merchandise items per product or size. These were configurable-in-code starting alert levels, not calculated forecasts or proven optimal reorder points. Actual reorder levels required sales-demand and supplier-lead-time information.
The system included a reporting feature that organized membership, payment, attendance, inventory, and sales information into separate reports for the gym admin to review.

The primary users of the system were the gym administrator, authorized staff, and registered gym members. The administrator could view member personal profiles without editing their personal details and manage membership operations, attendance, inventory, sales, staff accounts, phone pairings, activity logs, and reports. Authorized staff could record attendance, register walk-in members, process direct renewals and active-member plan changes using limited member lookup, record product sales, and review their own product-sale records. Both staff and administrators could approve or reject online registration and renewal requests, confirming in-person payment before approval. Staff could not view or edit existing member personal profiles. Members could view and update their own permitted personal details, access their membership status, attendance history and QR code, browse active products, and request renewal. Walk-in product purchases could be recorded without a member account.

Account creation included validation of required information, matching password confirmation, password-strength requirements, and duplicate email addresses or, where supported, usernames. Staff account registration collected first name, optional middle initial, and last name separately and combined them into the existing full-name record. Administrator and staff walk-in member forms used the same separate-name arrangement without introducing separate database name columns. Names containing numeric characters were rejected. Member password creation and updates used the implemented eight-character minimum; staff-account creation used a twelve-character minimum, with the applicable uppercase, lowercase, digit, and symbol requirements. Show/hide controls improved password entry without storing readable passwords. Administrator and staff accounts had to be active to use their protected functions. Members remained restricted to their own permitted personal information.

Administrator trusted-browser security. The current revision authorizes one trusted browser per administrator account for thirty days. First registration requires a fresh authenticator code. Returning to the same browser requires the password and automatic browser-key proof. A replacement browser requests approval from an eligible active trusted session and then requires fresh authenticator verification; successful replacement revokes the previous trust and dashboard/scanner scopes. If no eligible approving session is recently active, the implemented fallback uses fresh authenticator verification. Normal logout retains trust; explicit forget-device logout revokes it. Staff and member login remain role-specific. In-website notifications require an active connection; SMS and operating-system push are outside this implementation. Three private security tables support approval, trusted public keys and session challenges. Authenticator loss requires verified project-owner recovery. Migration and function deployment are evidenced by user-supplied CLI output; live authenticator and two-browser acceptance tests remain to be completed.

Dashboard sessions and attendance-scanner sessions are tracked separately. Ordinary session replacement affects the corresponding scope. Administrator trusted-browser transfer is an additional security operation: successful replacement of that trust revokes both previous dashboard and scanner scopes. Online pages check session ownership about every five seconds; suspended or offline pages check when they resume
or reconnect. The thirty-day phone-pairing period concerns the camera connection and is separate from administrator browser trust and operator authentication.

The activity-log implementation covered operational record changes and was extended to security and access events: rejected credential attempts, rate-limit rejections, member and scanner sign-ins and explicit sign-out requests, successful password updates, password-reset requests, and report-export requests. Administrators could filter and review these events; passwords, reset tokens, and report contents were excluded. Export logging represented a request rather than verified file-download completion, and closing a browser was not treated as a reliable explicit sign-out. The November 10, 2026 source changes required their database migration and authentication-function deployment before the expanded coverage could be claimed for production. Reset-request capture also depended on Supabase database Auth audit storage being enabled.

Member account access also included browser registration and approval. The system stored one registered browser per member account and required a new browser to obtain approval from the currently signed-in registered browser when that browser was available. Browser public keys, session challenges, and approval requests were maintained in separate private tables. These records were distinct from member profiles and phone-camera pairings. The migration and required functions were recorded as deployed; controlled member browser-acceptance testing remained pending.

The system was limited to Iron Grind Fitness Gym. It did not connect to other gyms, external stores, online payment gateways, banks, or mobile wallet services. It did not provide product reservations, AI-based workout or supplement recommendations, medical advice, or automated fitness coaching. Membership progress referred to the time remaining in a membership period and did not measure workout performance or physical changes. Traffic capacity and a maximum number of simultaneous users were not established by the available functional checks. A separate controlled load test and documented physical multi-phone validation remained necessary before making such performance claims.

The IronGrind: A Fitness Gym Membership and Operations Management System addressed the need to organize member records, membership applications and renewals, payments, attendance, inventory, and sales transactions.

Gym Owner and Admin of Iron Grind Fitness Gym. The system benefited the gym owner and admin by providing access to organized member profiles, membership records, applications, renewals, attendance logs, inventory information, sales transactions, and reports. It helped the admin retrieve records, monitor membership status, record in-person payments, manage products, and review each area of gym operations.

Gym Members. Members benefited from access to their membership information, membership-period progress, attendance history, and QR code through the member dashboard. They could also submit renewal requests online for authorized staff or administrator review.
Walk-in Customers. Walk-in customers benefited from having their completed in-person product purchases recorded accurately.

Organization: Iron Grind Fitness Gym. The system provided a centralized way to manage the gym’s membership and daily operational records. By organizing applications, renewals, attendance, inventory, sales, and reports, it supported more consistent recordkeeping and service.

Future Researchers. This study may serve as a reference for future researchers developing web-based systems for gym membership and operations management. Future studies may explore additional features, such as online payment integration or expanded mobile application capabilities, if these are needed and developed.
Administrator. An authorized user responsible for reviewing applications and managing member, attendance, inventory, sales, and report records.
Authentication. Verification of an account through Supabase Auth and the applicable administrator device-security checks before protected IronGrind access is authorized.
Authorization. The determination of which records and operations an authenticated user may access according to the permissions assigned in the system.

Authorized Staff. A user assigned a staff account to record attendance, register walk-in members, process direct membership renewals and plan changes, approve or reject online registration and renewal requests, and record in-person product sales within the access allowed by the system.
Centralized Database. The shared data store that organizes linked membership, attendance, inventory, and transaction records for IronGrind.
Digital Recordkeeping. The electronic storage and retrieval of gym information in place of relying only on paper forms, logbooks, and separate files.
Gym Management Application. A software application that supports the administration of gym services, such as membership records, attendance monitoring, inventory, and sales.
Gym Member. An individual with a member record in IronGrind. A linked sign-in account is separate and is available where the system has linked one.
Health Declaration. Health-related information provided by an applicant as part of membership registration; it is recorded for the gym's stated purposes and does not constitute a medical diagnosis.
Incomplete Attendance. A visit without a check-out whose check-in date is earlier than the current Philippine calendar date.
Information Quality. The accuracy, completeness, relevance, and clarity of information presented by a system, considered in this study as a concept for reviewing operational records.
Input Validation. Checks applied to submitted information, such as required fields, permitted formats, password requirements, and duplicate account identifiers.
Inventory. The recorded quantities of supplements and merchandise available at the gym, monitored using units appropriate to each product.

Membership Application. An online request from a prospective member to join the gym. A pending application awaits review by authorized staff or the administrator; a reviewed application retains its decision status.
Membership History. A record of membership events, including renewals, plan changes, and expired membership periods.
Membership Progress. A dashboard display showing the time remaining in a member’s recorded membership period.

Membership Renewal Request. A request submitted by an existing member to renew their membership. It may be submitted at any time and takes effect only after approval by authorized staff or the administrator. An active membership carries forward unused time, while an expired membership restarts on the approval date.
Membership Subscription. A recorded gym membership plan covering a defined period, with a start date and an expiration date.
Pending Pairing QR. An unexpired administrator-issued QR that reserves one phone-pairing slot until pairing is completed, ended, or expires.
Personal Information. Details recorded about an applicant, member, or operator, such as a name, contact information, and account information.
Phone Pairing. The administrator-authorized connection of a phone browser installation to attendance scanning for the recorded pairing period.

Progressive Web App (PWA). The installable browser-based attendance scanner that can be launched from a device home screen. Installation does not replace operator authentication, phone pairing, or the internet connection required to save attendance.
Point of Sale. The stage of an in-person purchase at which the gym records the products, quantities, and transaction amount; IronGrind records the transaction without providing a receipt.
PostgreSQL. The relational database technology underlying the Supabase database used to store IronGrind records.
QR Code. A two-dimensional machine-readable code assigned to a member and presented for authorized attendance scanning.
QR Code-Based Attendance Monitoring. The recording of a member check-in or check-out when an authorized administrator or staff member scans the member QR code.
Reporting Feature. A feature that organizes membership, payment, attendance, inventory, or sales information into reports available to authorized users according to their system role.
Role-Based Access Control. The assignment of system permissions according to administrator, staff, and member roles.
Row Level Security (RLS). Database rules used in Supabase to control which rows a user may read or modify.
Sales Transaction. A recorded in-person purchase containing the customer details, items or membership charges, quantities, and amount, as applicable.

Sensitive Personal Information. Under Republic Act No. 10173, information about a person's health is sensitive personal information. In IronGrind, this term refers to health-related declarations collected during registration and handled with restricted access.
Supabase. The hosted platform IronGrind uses for Auth and its PostgreSQL database. Configured Row Level Security policies and application role checks restrict permitted data access and operations.
System Quality. The reliability and usability of system functions, discussed as a concept in reviewing how IronGrind supports gym operations.
User Satisfaction. A user's assessment of their experience with the system, discussed as a concept rather than a measured result of this study.
User Session. The authenticated access period associated with a particular account sign-in and its permitted dashboard or attendance-scanner scope.

Trusted Browser. A browser profile and site origin whose public signing key is registered for an administrator account for the configured thirty-day trust period. Its private key remains in browser storage; this does not identify physical hardware.

Time-Based One-Time Password (TOTP). A short-lived code generated by an enrolled authenticator, used for administrator browser registration, replacement and the implemented recovery verification path.

Device Approval. An in-website decision by an eligible active trusted administrator session on another browser login request. Approval must be followed by fresh TOTP and successful device proof before trust is transferred.
Walk-in Customer. An individual who purchases gym products without using a registered member account.
Web-Based System. An application accessed through a web browser, allowing authorized users to use IronGrind through supported devices.
REVIEW OF RELATED LITERATURE AND STUDIES

This chapter reviews literature, applications, and studies relevant to gym membership, attendance monitoring, inventory management, and daily operations. Related Literature discusses technical concepts and frameworks that inform the project. Related Applications examines existing commercial gym management platforms, while Related Studies presents research on comparable systems. Together, these sources provide a basis for IronGrind: A Fitness Gym Membership and Operations Management System for Iron Grind Fitness Gym in Purok Mangga, Sulangon, Dapitan City, Zamboanga del Norte.

Supabase is a hosted platform whose projects include a dedicated PostgreSQL database, Auth and user management, Edge Functions, Realtime, and Storage (Supabase, n.d.-c). These services are relevant to IronGrind because its member profiles, applications, attendance, inventory, and sales records need a centralized data store and controlled access. IronGrind uses Supabase Auth to identify users and database authorization to restrict operations according to administrator, staff, and member roles. The platform is discussed here as supporting technology rather than as a competing gym management application.

A Quick Response (QR) Code is a standardized two-dimensional barcode symbology for encoding data (International Organization for Standardization, 2024). In IronGrind, a member presents a QR code so that an authorized administrator or staff member can record a check-in or check-out. The code supports member identification within the attendance workflow and replaces handwritten entry with a digital record. It does not perform biometric verification or operate an automated entrance gate. Supported phone cameras provide an additional scanning option under an authorized operator account.

The DeLone and McLean Information Systems Success Model examines information systems through dimensions such as system quality, information quality, service quality, use, user satisfaction, and net benefits. Al-Kofahi et al. (2025) reviewed 102 scholarly articles and conference papers indexed in Scopus and published between

2012 and 2021. Their weighted analysis identified information quality and user satisfaction as the strongest predictors among the model's internal variables. This framework is relevant to IronGrind because the system's value depends not only on the existence of its pages and database but also on whether its workflows are usable and provide dependable information for members and staff. The model provides a conceptual lens for examining IronGrind, not a measurement framework for this study.

The National Privacy Commission was constituted on March 7, 2016, under the Philippine Data Privacy Act of 2012 (National Privacy Commission, 2026). Section 11 of the Act states the principles of transparency, legitimate purpose, and proportionality; Section 3(l)(2) includes health information among sensitive personal information (Republic Act No. 10173, 2012). These provisions are relevant to IronGrind because the system stores account, contact, emergency contact, and health-related information.
Supabase (n.d.-b) describes Row Level Security as a database mechanism for restricting access to rows through policies.
Supabase (n.d.-d) explains that an Auth access token includes a session identifier associated with an Auth session record.
Supabase (n.d.-a) recommends reviewing query indexes and performing load testing, preferably in a staging environment, before production use.

Gymdesk presents a commercial approach to centralized gym administration. Its founder account describes the development of the platform from a side project into a service used by gyms (Gymdesk, 2025). Its relevance to IronGrind lies in bringing membership and operational information into an organized system. IronGrind applies that principle to a single gym through linked member, attendance, inventory, and transaction records. Features offered by a commercial platform are points of comparison; they do not establish which functions IronGrind implements or demonstrate the performance of the local system.
GymMaster advertises member management, billing, point-of-sale, inventory, access control, and online sign-ups (GymMaster, n.d.). GYMMANAGER advertises

customer management, sales, access control, facility operations, and analytics (GYMMANAGER, n.d.). These vendor-described functions provide comparison points for the commercial fitness-management sector; they are not independent evaluations of either product. IronGrind is designed around the workflows identified for one local gym and does not claim to implement every function advertised by these platforms, such as payment integrations, access-control hardware, or dedicated mobile applications.

Villanueva, Sevilla, and Verecio (2025) examined manual attendance, subscription monitoring, sales recording, and reporting at Olympic Fitness Gym in Tacloban City. Their study proposed a management system integrating QR code technology to address limitations in manual records and monitoring. It is relevant to IronGrind because both projects concern organizing membership and attendance information in a gym setting. IronGrind uses operator-scanned member QR codes and stores attendance separately from current membership details. The comparison supports the choice of related functions; it does not establish measured improvements for IronGrind.

Bulaclac, Pastorfide, Herrera, and Tambio (2025) developed a QR-enabled cashless payment and product-monitoring system for a Philippine fitness enterprise. They reported an 80% reduction in average transaction time, 95% accuracy in financial and inventory tracking, and a mean System Usability Scale score of 88 out of 100. These are findings for their evaluated system. The study is relevant to IronGrind because it examines linked operational records and QR-supported gym services. IronGrind records payments made in person and does not implement the cashless payment process studied by these authors. Its own accuracy, efficiency, and usability must be evaluated separately.

Babili (2026) presents GymFlow in an author-posted project report on an integrated fitness-center management system. The report describes membership administration, QR attendance, workout planning, payment recording, and progress analytics. It reports QR accuracy of 98.7%, processing time of 1.2 seconds, support for 200 concurrent users, and a System Usability Scale score of 85.6. These figures are author-reported results for GymFlow, not independently verified findings or results for IronGrind. The report provides a comparison for combining membership and attendance functions, while its workout
planning, analytics, and simulated payment gateway differ from the scope of IronGrind. The author-posted report should be distinguished from a peer-reviewed journal article.

The related literature identifies concepts that inform the design of IronGrind. A centralized database links operational records, authentication identifies users, and authorization limits permitted activities. QR codes support the attendance workflow, while the Information Systems Success Model provides a conceptual perspective on dependable information and usability. The privacy literature also highlights the need for careful handling of personal and health-related records. These concepts guide system design; they do not establish that the system has achieved measured improvements or verified legal compliance.

The related applications illustrate how commercial platforms organize gym services. Gymdesk, GymMaster, and GYMMANAGER combine membership administration with other operational functions. Their relevance lies in demonstrating existing approaches to centralized gym management. Their broader payment, access-control, and mobile capabilities are not automatically requirements of IronGrind, which is designed for the identified workflows of a single gym.

The related studies describe comparable efforts to organize gym operations. Villanueva et al. (2025) discuss attendance and subscription monitoring, Bulaclac et al. (2025) examine payment and product monitoring, and Babili (2026) presents an integrated QR-enabled gym system. These studies provide points of comparison for membership, attendance, inventory, and sales functions. Their reported results belong to their respective systems and are not evaluation results for IronGrind.

Taken together, the reviewed literature, applications, and studies support the development of a system tailored to Iron Grind Fitness Gym. IronGrind combines membership records, online application and renewal review, authorized staff operations, QR-based attendance, inventory using product-appropriate units, in-person transaction recording, and administrative reports. Payments are handled at the gym, and the system records transactions without providing receipts. The project applies these established
concepts to local operational requirements; any claims of improved accuracy, efficiency, or usability require evaluation of IronGrind itself.

The additional technical literature supports explicit input validation, active-role authorization, session management, and a clear distinction between verification and performance evaluation. In the system design, online request review remains available to authorized staff and administrators, phone-pairing reservations share the configured capacity, and attendance states reflect whether a check-out was recorded. These are implemented workflow rules whose correctness must be checked against the source code and database. This chapter discusses the methodology used to develop IronGrind: A Fitness Gym Membership and Operations Management System for Iron Grind Fitness Gym in Purok Mangga, Sulangon, Dapitan City, Zamboanga del Norte. IronGrind is a web application with an installable attendance-scanner component. This chapter describes the development process, system requirements, design, data organization, and evaluation procedures. The system organizes membership applications and records, membership periods and renewals, attendance, products, sales, reports, and activity review. Its development is organized using Agile, with work planned and delivered incrementally. Proposed evaluation activities are distinguished from results that have not yet been collected.

Agile is an iterative system-development approach in which requirements guide the work, features are built in manageable increments, and the results of testing and review guide subsequent work. As shown in Figure 1, the process begins by planning IronGrind's workflows and priorities and designing the related pages, forms, data relationships, and access permissions. The team then develops a selected group of features and tests them against their requirements. Deployment in the cycle means preparing and checking an

increment in its intended environment; review considers the test findings and any feedback actually collected. Those findings return to planning and help determine what to refine or build next. This cycle applies to the system's membership applications and renewals, attendance, inventory, sales, and reports. The final Launch stage represents release of the approved system for operational use after the required increments have been verified. Figure 1 describes this project's workflow; it does not claim use of a specific Agile framework or a fixed iteration length. Evaluation results are reported only after the planned evaluation activities have been completed.

Pavlović (2018) discusses the importance of organizational support, consistent practices, and adequate skills and training when adopting Agile. This perspective informed the choice of approach for the study and supports treating iterative development as a structured process requiring planning and review. The phases shown in Figure 1 organize development tasks for IronGrind, including its membership, attendance, inventory, sales, and reporting features.

Requirements planning identifies separate workflows for applicants, members, administrators, and authorized staff. Requirements cover online applications subject to authorized staff or administrator review, direct counter registration and membership changes, QR attendance, product inventory, transaction recording, reporting, staff accounts, phone pairing, and activity logs. Acceptance criteria include role permissions, required inputs, stock and membership updates, and rejection of unauthorized operations. These criteria guide each development increment.

Using the prioritized requirements, the team designs or refines the corresponding user workflows, page layouts, forms, reports, data relationships, and role permissions. For example, the design distinguishes pending applications from approved member records, keeps attendance as a separate operational record, and stores sales with their itemized lines. The architecture, use-case, and data-flow figures in this chapter summarize how these parts fit together. These designs are then represented in prototypes so that the intended workflows can be reviewed before or during construction.

If a test identifies an issue, the team corrects it and checks it again; unresolved or newly discovered needs are recorded for prioritization. Once the increment passes the required checks, it can be prepared in the intended environment and reviewed. The data-process model follows information from an actor, through an authorized system function, to the records it reads or changes. Applicant registration and renewal requests are reviewed before they create or update member and payment records. Read the diagrams together to follow the same operation at different levels. Figure 2 is the context diagram. It contains one process, numbered 0, representing IronGrind and three external actor groups: Member / Applicant, Administrator, and Authorized Staff. Databases, authentication services, and phone-pairing storage remain internal to the system boundary.

The Member/Applicant provides inputs such as sign-in credentials, registration details, membership applications, renewal requests, and profile updates. In return, the system provides outputs including authentication results, application statuses, membership details, attendance history, the active product catalog, and account information.
The Administrator provides application review decisions, membership and inventory updates, sales entries, staff account controls, phone-pairing administration, and report or activity-log queries.

The system returns the corresponding records, status confirmations, account information, activity logs, and reports. Authorized staff provide attendance scans, walk-in registration details, direct renewal and plan-change inputs, online request decisions, and
product sales entries; they receive only the confirmations and records permitted for their role.

Figure 2 defines the external boundary of the IronGrind Membership and Operations Management System using a Gane-Sarson context diagram. Process 0 represents the system as a single unit, while the rectangles identify its three external user groups: Member / Applicant, Administrator, and Authorized Staff. Each directed arrow describes information entering or leaving the system. An arrow pointing toward Process 0 represents submitted data or a request; an arrow pointing toward an external entity represents information or a result returned to that user group. The diagram provides an overview of responsibilities and information exchange, rather than the sequence of screens, database operations, or implementation steps.

The Member / Applicant entity combines two stages of the customer relationship: a person applying for membership and an existing member using personal account services. Its incoming flow consists of credentials, registration details, renewal requests, and permitted profile changes. Registration details describe the information submitted for review; submission alone does not mean that membership has been approved. A renewal request concerns an existing membership and must be reviewed before its result is applied. Permitted profile changes concern the signed-in member's own editable personal information and do not include authority to approve requests, alter product stock, record sales, or modify another member's account.

The corresponding outgoing flow returns sign-in and application results, the member's own membership information and QR code, attendance history, and the active product catalog. Access results indicate whether account access is permitted, while application results communicate the recorded review status. Membership information enables the member to check the plan, status, and applicable membership dates. The QR code supports identification during an authorized operator's attendance scan; showing the QR code does not give the member attendance-recording privileges. Attendance history is limited to the member's own visits. The catalog allows products to be viewed, while product-sale entries are handled through the administrator or authorized staff workflow rather than through a member checkout process.
The Administrator entity submits credentials, application and renewal review decisions, membership operations, product and stock updates, product-sale entries, staff and device

instructions, and report or activity-log queries. These inputs represent separate authorized requests rather than one combined transaction. Membership operations include supported counter registration, renewal, and plan changes. Staff controls concern staff accounts, while device controls concern the supported scanner and trusted-browser arrangements. Queries retrieve information; they do not themselves change the underlying business records.

The system returns administrator access results, operation confirmations, member and staff information, device states, reports, and recorded activity. The return flow lets the administrator confirm a submitted operation or inspect information within the permitted scope. Viewing an existing member personal profile remains read-only. Membership approval, renewal, and plan changes are operational responsibilities and do not authorize editing that member personal profile.

The Authorized Staff entity exchanges credentials, counter details, request-review decisions, QR scans, and product-sale entries. After staff identity and active-account status have been verified, the permitted tasks include walk-in member registration, limited member lookup for counter transactions, direct renewal, active-member plan changes, review of online registration and renewal requests, attendance scanning, and product-sale recording. A member lookup supplies the limited details needed to select the correct person for an authorized transaction; it is not general access to the member's personal profile. Staff review decisions are based on the request information made available by the staff interface. The QR scan flow submits a member identifier for the system to validate and record the applicable attendance result.

The system returns staff access results, pending-request information or status, counter-operation results, scan results, permitted attendance records, and the staff operator's own product-sale records. These outputs support the assigned task and allow its result to be checked. Staff access does not include viewing or editing existing member profiles, maintaining inventory, administering staff accounts or phone pairings, or opening administrator reports and activity logs. The narrower staff outputs distinguish the staff workspace from the administrator workspace even when both roles can initiate a supported membership or attendance operation. The diagram represents these information exchanges;
authentication, role checks, database policies, and authorized functions enforce the access boundaries in the implementation.

Walk-in customers are not drawn as a separate direct system user because an administrator or authorized staff operator enters their counter transactions. The customer supplies the relevant details to that operator, who submits the supported system entry and receives its confirmation. A saved sale or membership transaction is an internal operational record; the confirmation does not establish that the system issues a customer receipt. Likewise, the context diagram's arrows represent information exchange rather than a physical payment channel, an online payment gateway, or the transfer of goods.

The actor-specific arrows are essential to interpreting User Management and attendance correctly. An administrator's profile-view query returns a read-only member profile. A member's personal-change request affects only their own permitted personal details. Staff arrows identify counter and attendance operations and do not include a profile query or personal-detail edit. Internal writes caused by registration, renewal, or server-side account provisioning describe the effects of an authorized operation; they are not a grant of general editing access to the underlying table. Authentication, role checks, database policies, and authorized functions support these boundaries even when different operations use the same data store.

Processes 8.0 and 9.0 have distinct outputs. Generate Reports reads operational records to produce the selected report and its supported preview or export. Activity Logs reads previously recorded events and returns the administrator's filtered results. Staff-account changes occur under User Management, and phone-pairing changes occur under QR Attendance administration. Their events may appear in the log, but the log viewer does not perform those changes. This separation prevents the model from treating monitoring an operation as permission to execute it.

Supabase Auth verifies credentials and establishes the user session. The system reads the profile role and active-account state to route the account to the administrator, staff, or member interface. Authorization is enforced through database policies, role-checked functions, and Edge Functions, rather than relying on page visibility alone.

2.0 Review Online Applications. Applicants submit registration details and health declarations to membership_applications. Authorized staff and administrators review online requests and approve or reject them. Approval creates or links the member record, updates the application status, and records the applicable membership payment through sales and sale_items. Direct walk-in registration follows process 3.0 as a separate counter operation.

3.0 User Management. Administrators can view member profiles but cannot edit their personal information. They perform authorized membership operations and create or activate/deactivate staff accounts through authorized services. Members can retrieve and update only their own permitted personal details. Staff have a separate labeled counter flow: walk-in registration, limited member lookup, direct renewal, and active-member plan change. Staff cannot view or edit existing member profiles. Account rows created by the registration service describe backend storage, not profile-editing permission granted to staff. Membership changes record applicable member, history, sales, and sale-item updates.

4.0 Review Online Renewals. Members submit renewal requests to membership_applications. Authorized staff and administrators approve or reject these requests. An approved renewal preserves unused time by extending an active membership from its current expiry date; an expired membership restarts on approval. Approval updates the member, history, application status, and membership transaction records. Direct counter renewals by an administrator or staff operator belong to process 3.0 and are separate from the online Requests approval workflow.

5.0 Record and View Attendance. An authorized administrator or staff operator scans a member QR code with a supported computer or phone camera. The database validates the operator and member, checks for an open visit, and records check-in or check-out in attendance. recorded_by and checked_out_by identify the operators for each event. Private attendance_scan_requests records support duplicate-request protection. Paired phones additionally use administrator-managed pairing sessions and policy; pairing does not replace operator authentication. Members can read their own attendance history. Authorized staff and administrators read attendance within their permitted scope. Administrator-only phone-pairing creation, settings and removal belong to this attendance

workflow. Staff and members do not receive those administration controls. A phone without an active pairing displays Phone not paired and must scan an administrator-generated pairing QR before member attendance scanning. The setup QR expires after ten minutes; successful pairing lasts thirty days from pairing time unless removed earlier. Reopening the camera does not renew that period. Missing check-outs from a previous Philippine calendar date are labeled Incomplete; current-day open visits remain checked in. The display does not invent a check-out time.

Phone pairing capacity counts both paired devices and unexpired pending QR reservations. At the initial two-slot limit, the permitted combinations are two paired phones, one paired phone plus one pending QR, or two pending QRs. Scanning a reserved QR completes that reservation without allocating another slot. Creating a further QR is blocked at capacity, while an existing pending QR remains available to scan. Each browser installation has its own identifier; another installation cannot take over an assigned QR. The device label is descriptive information and does not provide hardware attestation. An expired, removed, or unsuccessful pairing is not counted as a completed device connection.

6.0 Manage Inventory and Catalog. Administrators maintain product details, prices, stock, product forms, and active or archived state. Powder supplements support weight units; drinkable supplements support volume units; capsules and tablets use pieces or boxes; other supplements and merchandise use items. Sale processing converts compatible quantities and deducts stock using the configured inventory units. Members browse active products, and staff obtain the permitted catalog needed for sales; these read operations do not grant inventory-maintenance permission.

Administrators and staff record in-person product purchases for members or walk-in customers. The sale operation validates quantities and product status, writes sales and sale_items, and deducts product stock. Membership charges are recorded through the membership operations in processes 2.0 to 4.0. The database retains the existing receipt_number field as an internal transaction identifier. The documented operating process does not provide customers with receipts.

Administrators select a report type and period to retrieve the relevant operational records. Supported outputs include preview, print layout, individual PDFs, and combined ZIP export. This reporting process does not manage staff access, phone pairings, or activity-log filters.

Administrators review database-recorded actions using date, account, action, and area filters and pagination. Logs include recorded staff-account changes and phone-pairing events. The interface reads activity_logs; it does not create staff accounts, alter pairing settings, or modify the recorded events. Those operations occur in User Management or QR Attendance and produce their own log entries.

Member / Applicant represents a prospective applicant and an existing member at their respective stages of interaction with the gym. This actor is associated with User Login, Membership Application, User Management, Renewals, QR Attendance, and Product & Inventory. They do not give staff general access to member profiles, inventory maintenance, staff-account administration, phone-pairing administration, administrator reports, or activity logs. Administrator is associated with all nine functions and performs the operational and supervisory actions permitted by the administrator
workflow. Its broader participation still respects the implemented restriction that member personal profiles are viewed without editing their personal details.

Membership Application covers online registration submission and its review. The applicant supplies the required registration information and receives the recorded application status. An authorized staff member or administrator reviews the limited pending-request details and records an approval or rejection. Approval is performed through an authorized server-side operation that rechecks the operator and pending state, prevents repeat processing, and creates or links the appropriate member and membership transaction records. The applicant's association represents submitting and checking the request, while the operator associations represent review and processing. User Management includes role-specific account, personal-profile, and counter membership responsibilities. Administrators view member profiles without editing their personal details and control supported staff-account access. Members alone update their own permitted personal-profile details. Staff register walk-in members and process direct renewals or active-plan changes using limited lookup information. Those counter operations create or update the records required for the authorized membership transaction; they do not provide a general member-profile viewer or an existing-profile editing function. All three User Management associations are therefore intentional and match the functional

All three actors are connected because they participate in this functional area, but only the administrator maintains inventory. Catalog access does not establish an online member checkout, authorize a stock adjustment, or permit a staff member to change product information.

sale unit, quantity, price, and available stock, records the sale and line items, and applies the corresponding stock deduction.
