Database policies, active-role checks, authorized functions, and server-side services enforce the restrictions described here. The system-flow discussion that follows explains how these responsibilities operate together in the implemented workflows.

End-to-end system flow. Each protected operation begins with authentication and an active-role check. Page visibility alone does not authorize a database change; database policies, role-checked functions, or authorized server-side services validate privileged operations.

1. Applicant account and request. A prospective member creates an account with email and password through Supabase Auth before the online application is reviewed. The application is stored separately with its applicant account link and a pending status. Submission alone does not create an approved member record or active membership.

2. Review and membership activation. Authorized staff or an administrator loads limited pending-request details, confirms that payment was received at the gym, and chooses approve or reject. The server rechecks the active role, locks the pending request, and prevents a second review. Rejection records the decision. Approval of registration creates the member record linked to the existing Auth account; approval of renewal updates the membership dates. Approved requests also record the membership transaction, and renewals add a membership-history event.

3. Member self-service. A member signs in with email to view their own membership, progress, QR code, attendance history, and active catalog. They may update permitted personal details and submit a renewal request. A member can access only their own records; administrator profile viewing is read-only, and staff have no member-profile viewing or editing permission.

4. Counter and attendance operations. Administrator and staff walk-in registration collect first name, optional middle initial and last name, combine them into the existing full-name value, and submit the membership details to an authorized service. Direct renewal and active-plan change use limited lookup rather than a profile screen; staff confirm the selected member, current plan, payment amount and replacement dates before saving. Attendance uses a member QR or staff name/Gmail lookup with explicit selection. The service checks the member and open visit before recording check-in/out and the responsible operator. An earlier-date visit without check-out is shown as Incomplete without inventing an exit time. Phone pairing, operator authentication and PWA installation are separate steps.

5. Products, sales, and oversight. Administrators maintain the catalog, prices, product units, stock, and active state. Members and staff read only the catalog permitted for their role. When an operator records an in-person product sale, the service validates the item, unit, and available stock, saves the sale and line item, and deducts the quantity. IronGrind records payment at the gym but does not issue a customer receipt. Staff may review their own product sales. Administrators separately generate reports and read filtered activity logs; the log viewer does not perform the logged operations.

Supabase Auth verifies credentials. Members sign in with the email address on their account; staff and administrators use their assigned usernames. Member registration collects an email and password, not a separate username, and the member dashboard displays the member's full name. The profile role and active-account state determine administrator, staff, or member access, with protected operations checked by server-side authorization. New member registration uses a visible password-strength indicator and blocks passwords that do not meet the Strong requirements: 8 to 128 characters, uppercase and lowercase letters, at least one digit, and at least one symbol. Confirmation must match the selected password. Auth and the member-creation service enforce the password policy on the server; staff-account creation uses a minimum of 12 characters with the same character requirements. Existing sign-in forms continue to accept account credentials without imposing registration validation on login.

Administrator device authorization is part of User Login rather than an additional main function. Password authentication establishes an Auth session but does not by itself authorize an administrator dashboard or scanner session. The server checks the active role, application scope, current trusted public key and authorized session mapping. A session may access protected operations only after the applicable device-verification workflow completes. Staff and member login retain their role-specific checks.

First registration and return visits. The genuine administrator privately enrolls a TOTP authenticator when required and verifies a fresh code to register the first trusted browser. The browser creates an ECDSA P-256 key pair and retains a non-extractable private CryptoKey in IndexedDB; the server stores the public JWK. Trust lasts thirty days from registration. A later password login in the same browser and origin proves possession of that key automatically, without requesting a code on every login. Routine reuse does not extend the trust period. This is browser-profile trust, not a hardware identity: a different browser, origin, cleared storage or unavailable key can require registration again.

Replacement while another trusted session is active. A different browser submits a session-bound approval request after password verification. The currently active trusted browser receives an in-website notification and may approve or deny it. The requesting

browser must then complete fresh TOTP verification and sign its server-issued challenge. Approval alone does not authorize access. A successful server transaction replaces the trusted key and revokes the previous dashboard and attendance scopes; cancellation, denial or failed verification preserves the previous trust. Requests expire after two minutes, and signing challenges after ten minutes.

Availability, logout and recovery. The application polls for approval notifications while the trusted page is active; a heartbeat within two minutes determines whether an eligible approving session is recently active. This is not SMS, operating-system push, or proof that a physical device is online. When no eligible approving session is available, fresh authenticator verification provides the implemented replacement path. Normal logout retains browser trust, while Log out and forget this device revokes it. Lost authenticator access requires verified project-owner recovery. There is no password-only bypass or custom backup-code recovery. Device-signature authorization does not itself change the Auth JWT assurance level to AAL2.

Implementation and evidence. admin-device-trust.js coordinates browser-key proof, admin-device-approval.js handles approval notifications, and admin-mfa.js performs enrollment and fresh authenticator verification. The admin-device-trust Edge Function validates the signed-in account and session, verifies the signature and fresh TOTP evidence, and calls service-only completion functions. Database policies and session guards enforce the result independently of visible dialogs. User-supplied CLI output confirms application of migrations through 20261110000004 and deployment of admin-device-trust. These outputs do not establish successful physical two-browser transfer, authenticator use or matching Vercel frontend deployment; those remain acceptance checks.

Usernames and email addresses are checked for duplicates without regard to capitalization or surrounding spaces. Registration shows availability feedback and rejects identifiers already in use; server checks support this validation. Dashboard and attendance-scanner sessions are tracked as separate scopes. Ordinary replacement affects its own scope, while successful administrator trusted-browser transfer explicitly revokes both old scopes. Online pages check ownership about every five seconds and return to sign-in when

replaced; offline or suspended pages check on resumption or reconnection. Trust transfer and explicit forget-device revocation are additional administrator security controls, not ordinary scope-only replacement.

2. Register and Submit Membership Application. An applicant creates an account using an email address and password, then submits personal and health information for review by authorized staff or the administrator. Name fields accept names containing letters and reject numeric characters.

3. Review Membership Applications. Authorized staff and the administrator review pending application summaries and approve or reject requests according to the gym's criteria, confirming in-person payment before approval.

4. Create or Link Member Account. Approval by an authorized staff member or administrator links an online application to the approved member record. Direct walk-in registration by an authorized administrator or staff operator uses a server-side Edge Function to create the appropriate Auth, profile, member, and payment records.
5. View Application status at Login. The User can check the current status of their membership application when signing in to see if it is pending, approved, or rejected.
6. View Membership Dashboard. This function allows the User to access their personalized dashboard, displaying their active membership plan, time-based progress, and their unique QR code.

7. User Management. The administrator can view member profiles but cannot update their personal details. Only members update their own permitted personal profile fields. Administrator membership operations, staff-account controls, and membership-history review are separate from personal-profile editing. Staff have no member-profile viewing or editing function.

8. Record Membership Attendance. An administrator or authorized staff operator scans a member QR using a supported camera. Staff can also search by member name or Gmail, select the matching member and record attendance. The service validates the supplied member identifier and visit state, records check-in/out and the responsible operator, and returns the result.
9. View Personal Attendance History. A member can view their own visit dates and recorded check-in and check-out times. A visit without a recorded check-out does not display an invented exit time.

10. View and Update Own Profile. A member can view their own profile and update permitted personal details. The administrator may view member profiles but cannot edit them. Staff have no access to member profile viewing or editing.
11. Browse Active Product Catalog. The User can view the available supplements and merchandise sold by the gym.
12. Manage Products and Inventory. The Admin can add, update, and monitor the product catalog, ensuring that merchandise stock quantities and supplement details are accurate.

Low-stock policy and catalog organization. The administrator inventory view separates selling price from stock on hand and shows low-stock alerts in the configured stock unit. Powder alerts use 1,000 g for protein; 250 g for creatine, pre-workout, amino-acid and vitamin powders; and 500 g for other powders. Liquid alerts use 1,000 ml; individually sold capsules/tablets use 30 pieces; boxed supplements use four boxes; other supplement items use ten items; and merchandise uses four items per product/size. Product form and sale unit take precedence over supplement type. Pounds and ounces are converted before comparison, so the same physical quantity has the same alert status regardless of entry unit. Values at or below the threshold trigger an alert; zero stock is distinguished as unavailable. Thresholds are starting policy values in application code, not stored threshold columns or demand-based reorder forecasts. Staff catalog sections separate Supplements into Powders, Capsules, Tablets, Liquids/drinks and Other, with Merchandise separately. Saved form metadata determines grouping; legacy gram or milliliter products can use a unit-based fallback, while an unidentified form remains Other.

13. Record Product Sale. An administrator or staff operator records an in-person product purchase, with validated quantities, saved sales and line items, and corresponding stock deduction. Staff can review their own product-sale records. No receipt provision is included in the documented operating process.

14. Submit Membership Renewal Request. This function allows a member to submit a renewal request at any time, subject to approval by authorized staff or the administrator. If approved while the membership is active, the new membership duration is added after the current expiry date. If approved after expiration, the renewed period begins on the approval date.
15. View Dashboard and Operational Reports. The Admin can view a summarized dashboard showing active members, daily sales, and attendance, as well as access specific operational reports.
16. Export Reports. This function allows the Admin to generate, download, or print detailed reports for record-keeping and business analysis.

17. Activity Logs and Related Administration. The administrator reviews recorded activity through the Activity Logs use case. Staff-account changes are performed under User Management; phone-pairing changes are performed under QR Attendance administration. These operations generate log entries but are not performed inside the read-only log viewer. Business approval or expiry email notifications are not included as implemented use cases.

Expanded audit coverage and presentation. Operational writes continue to generate database audit events. The security extension adds server-recorded failed credential attempts and rate-limit rejections, member and scanner session events, successful password updates, recovery requests and report-export requests. Failed attempts are attributed to an unverified visitor rather than assumed to be the account owner. Password-change events identify the affected account without storing its password or hash in the activity log; the authenticated actor is used when available, otherwise the authentication service is shown. Recovery requests do not prove that the requester owns an account or that an email was delivered. Report export means a request, not verified browser-download completion. The administrator viewer keeps action labels distinct from descriptions and places technical identifiers and changed-field names inside expandable Details. Account, grouped category, action and Philippine date-range filters operate with server-side pagination. Searches and routine page views are not comprehensively logged. Database and Edge Function
deployment, plus enabled Auth database audit storage for recovery requests, are required for this expanded coverage.

Figure 5 presents the public-schema relationship overview for IronGrind. It contains twelve public application tables and the eighteen foreign-key relationships declared on those tables. The auth.users card represents a referenced Supabase-managed identity table and is not counted as an application-owned public table. Selected key and descriptive attributes are shown to keep the overview manageable; the data dictionary that follows provides the complete documented field definitions.

The central membership records connect account identity, applications, current membership, visits, transactions, and membership history. A membership application can refer to an existing member when the request concerns that member. Conversely, the optional unique members.application_id identifies the application from which a member record originated. These are separate foreign keys with different purposes: one member may have multiple requests, while a particular source application can be linked to at most one member through the unique source-application field. Walk-in members do not require an online source application.

Attendance records belong to members and retain the identities of the operators who recorded check-in and check-out. Sales headers may refer to members and identify the processing account, while sale_items provides the itemized lines of a sale and any associated product reference. Membership history preserves recorded membership changes. Scanner-session and scan-event tables describe paired attendance communication, and the pairing-policy table records the configured capacity policy. The activity_logs table is shown without an invented foreign-key relationship: an actor identifier recorded in a log is not, by itself, evidence of a declared database constraint.

PK identifies a primary key, FK a foreign key, and UQ an individually unique key. In crow-foot notation, a circle means zero is permitted, a bar denotes one, and the fork denotes many; the endpoint symbols must be read together. Solid connectors link the public application tables. Dashed blue-gray connectors identify references to managed authentication identities; this line style is a visual grouping choice and does not imply weaker referential enforcement. A line crossing does not create a relationship.
This figure intentionally covers the public schema rather than the entire application-owned database. The documented full model contains twenty-one application tables, 224

fields, and thirty-three declared foreign keys: twelve public tables and nine private supporting tables. The private structures support attendance requests, login attempts, scoped account sessions, and administrator/member device authorization. Their definitions remain in the data dictionary and separate security reference materials. The overview describes stored relationships, not role permissions or proof of production deployment; its schema baseline comes from the supplied export and checked-in migrations rather than a new live-database inspection.

The data dictionary uses five columns: Field Name, Field Type, Length / Precision / Scale, Key, and Description and Validation Details. Declared character limits and numeric precision and scale are reported separately from the base type. Not declared identifies text, array, or JSON types without a declared character maximum; N/A identifies types without a length parameter. PK, FK, and UQ identify primary, foreign, and individually unique keys. Descriptions retain nullability, referenced keys, referential actions, composite constraints, defaults, identity generation, and relevant checks. These definitions describe the documented migration model rather than a new live-database inspection.

The system uses registration, profile, renewal, member, inventory, sales, staff-account, and phone-pairing forms. Members submit online registration or renewal information and maintain their permitted profile details. Administrators review online requests, maintain products and stock, and manage staff and pairing access. Authorized staff use counter forms for walk-in registration, direct renewal, active-member plan change, and product purchases, and use Requests approval for online registration and renewal decisions. Attendance uses camera scanning under an authorized operator account. Completed payments and purchases are recorded as transactions; receipts are not provided to customers. Required fields, validation, and server-side role checks support consistent data entry.

The Create Staff Account form collects first name, optional middle initial, and last name in separate inputs. It formats a supplied initial with a period and combines the parts into the existing full_name value; separate name columns are not introduced. The form also checks username and Gmail availability, phone format, password strength, and matching confirmation. Staff directory access and activation controls remain administrator-only. The Requests approval view separately presents pending online registration and renewal summaries for authorized staff and administrator decisions, with in-person payment confirmation before approval.

Figure 63 presents the original ten-week development schedule for IronGrind, from August 24 to October 28, 2026. The activity and date columns identify the work assigned to each scheduled week. As clarified by the proponents, Planning occupies Weeks 1-4 and consists of identifying a potential client, conducting the first client interview to identify problems and needs, project conceptualization, and drafting the proposal. Design occupies Weeks 5-8 and covers interface design, prototype development, client feedback, and refinement. Development occupies Weeks 9-10 and covers frontend, backend, database, API, and supporting work alongside the project chapters. The four planning labels reflect the activities reported by the proponents. The existing date ranges are retained as schedule assignments and do not independently establish the actual completion dates of those activities.

Each colored bar locates an activity within its assigned planned week. The chart does not record actual completion, measured effort, evaluation outcomes, or production readiness. Its three phase groups organize the original schedule, while the Agile methodology describes how development and refinement can repeat within and beyond that plan. Later repository revisions and deployment evidence must be reported separately rather than retroactively treated as work completed within the original ten weeks.
